title: Arts in the Age of Data: skill trees
intro: Four skill trees: the data project, the critical lens, the tools and the teamwork. Pick a badge to see its skills, tick what you've learned, and watch the trees light up. Your read-out below turns it into language for CVs, applications and interviews.

extension.label: Extension
extension.note: Optional, and encouraged: skills that go beyond what the unit teaches, for you to pick up independently.

hero.label: All Round Data Hero
hero.blurb: Every badge in all four trees.

stages.label: Set up
stages.blurb: Form the team, pick a topic, plan.

setup.question: Why this topic, and whose story does the data tell?

find.question: Who collected this data, and what does it leave out?

prepare.question: What assumptions are you building in as you clean and combine?

analyse.question: Could something else explain this pattern?

visualise.question: Does your design inform, or does it spin?

tell.question: What do the findings mean, and for whom?

lens-ai-data.label: What did the AI learn from?

lens-ai-power.label: AI, capital and power

team-act-feedback.label: Act on feedback

team-deadline.label: Meet a group deadline

team-midpoint.label: Lead the mid-point review

viz-hierarchy.label: Lead with the key message
viz-hierarchy.desc: Give the most important finding the most visual weight.

report-captions.label: Title and caption every chart
report-captions.desc: Give each chart a title that says what it shows, and a source line.

lens-define.label: Define the age of data
lens-define.desc: Explain what is meant by the age of data, and when and why it began.

lens-essay.label: Write about the age of data
lens-essay.desc: Contribute to the study of the age of data in an essay of your own.

references.label: Reference lists and notes
references.desc: Cite your sources in notes and a reference list so readers can check them.

map-points.label: Create points from coordinates
map-points.desc: Plot places as points from their latitude and longitude.

interactive-viz.label: Interactive or animated charts
interactive-viz.desc: Build charts readers can explore, or that move to show change.

badges.label: Launch Data Project
badges.blurb: Choose a topic and plan the project.
badges.cv: Scoped a group data project: chose a topic, defined the problem and research questions, decided what to measure and set up a project plan and shared workspace.
badges.story: Tell me how your group chose its topic and turned it into a question data could answer. What trade-offs did you make?
badges.next: Practise writing a one-paragraph project brief in plain English: it is how most workplace projects begin.

badges.label: Data Gatherer
badges.cv: Located, assessed and extracted data from published reports and official sources, converting it into analysis-ready formats.
badges.story: Describe how you tracked down the data your project needed. What did you do when it wasn't in the form you wanted?
badges.next: Get to know the main UK sources (ONS, data.gov.uk, the UK Data Service) so you know where to look first in any new role.

badges.label: Data Creator
badges.blurb: Build data that doesn't exist yet.
badges.cv: Created new datasets by digitising printed or visual sources, assembling time series from several releases and pulling custom extracts from online databases.
badges.story: Tell me about a time the data you needed didn't exist yet. How did you build it, and how did you check its accuracy?
badges.next: Digitise a small archival or historical source of your own: it makes a strong portfolio piece for research, heritage and archive roles.

badges.label: Advanced Data Types
badges.blurb: JSON, maps, text and survey weights.
badges.cv: Worked with non-standard data formats, including JSON, shapefiles, text data and weighted survey data.
badges.story: Describe a dataset that was harder to work with than a normal spreadsheet. What did you have to learn to use it?
badges.next: An introductory Python or R course is the natural next step: these formats are where code starts to pay off.

badges.label: Wrangler
badges.cv: Cleaned, structured and combined raw datasets, documenting sources and field definitions so the work could be checked and reused.
badges.story: Describe a problem you found while cleaning data, such as missing values, inconsistent names or a misleading field. How did you spot it, and what did you do?
badges.next: Keep a short data dictionary for every project: it is standard practice in analyst roles.

badges.label: Advanced Wrangler
badges.cv: Validated and integrated three or more datasets, managing storage and versions and checking combined results for consistency.
badges.story: Tell me about combining several datasets. What went wrong when you joined them, and how did you find out?
badges.next: A free introduction to SQL would show you how organisations manage data at scale.

badges.label: Analyst Foundations
badges.cv: Calculated totals and percentages accurately and distinguished between categorical and numerical data before analysing them.
badges.story: Tell me about a time a simple calculation mattered. How did you make sure it was right?
badges.next: Many graduate employers use numerical reasoning tests: practise these alongside your project work.

badges.label: Common visualisations
badges.cv: Created clear column, line and pie charts, formatting axes, legends, colour and annotation for readability.
badges.story: Show me a chart you improved. What did the default version get wrong, and what did you change?
badges.next: Every time you make a chart, ask what you can remove: it is the quickest way to improve.

badges.label: Summarise data
badges.cv: Summarised datasets with averages, ranges, percentiles and frequency counts, choosing the right measure for the data.
badges.story: When did choosing the median rather than the mean, or the reverse, change the story your data told?
badges.next: Try summarising a public dataset in five numbers and two sentences: it is a common task in analyst interviews.

badges.label: Design principles
badges.cv: Applied design principles, including audience, low-ink design and appropriate chart choice, to make visualisations clear and honest.
badges.story: Tell me about designing something for a particular audience. How did knowing who they were change your choices?
badges.next: Collect three charts you admire and three you don't, and write a line on why for each.

badges.label: Compare datasets
badges.cv: Compared datasets using measures of spread such as variance and standard deviation.
badges.story: Tell me about two groups or places you compared. How did you decide whether the difference was meaningful?
badges.next: Find out what a confidence interval is: it is the natural next step from standard deviation.

badges.label: Change over time
badges.cv: Measured change over time using percentage change, average growth, index numbers, inflation adjustment and trendlines.
badges.story: Describe a trend you measured. How did you make sure you were comparing like with like across the years?
badges.next: Use the ONS inflation calculators and indices to practise real-terms comparisons on topics you care about.

badges.label: Infographic design
badges.blurb: Plan and lay out an infographic.
badges.cv: Designed an infographic with a clear structure, visual hierarchy and flow, planned from a wireframe.
badges.story: Walk me through how you planned your infographic's layout. What did you put first, and why?
badges.next: Keep a PDF of your infographic to share in applications and interviews.

badges.label: Mapping
badges.cv: Created thematic and point maps of data at city, UK and global scales.
badges.story: Tell me about a map you made. What did showing the data geographically reveal that a chart didn't?
badges.next: If map-making appeals, try QGIS, which is free and used widely in government, planning and heritage.

badges.label: Detect relationships
badges.cv: Tested relationships between variables with scatter graphs and the correlation coefficient (r), and explained the difference between correlation and causation.
badges.story: Tell me about a relationship you found in your data. How did you avoid claiming more than it showed?
badges.next: Look for a correlation reported in the news and work out what else could explain it.

badges.label: Causation
badges.cv: Applied linear regression and contingency coefficients to explore causal questions, and assessed the limits of causal claims.
badges.story: Tell me about a time you tried to establish cause and effect. What stopped you being certain?
badges.next: An introductory statistics or quantitative methods course would build directly on this.

badges.label: Integrated report: text & data viz
badges.blurb: Combine writing and charts in one piece.
badges.cv: Produced an integrated, fully referenced report combining concise written analysis with titled, captioned data visualisations for a non-specialist audience.
badges.story: Walk me through your final infographic. Who was it for, and what design and writing decisions did you make for them?
badges.next: Rewrite your report's key message as a 100-word briefing note: a format used across government, policy and business.

badges.label: Advanced data viz storytelling
badges.cv: Developed my data storytelling by recreating landmark visualisations, learning from current work and building interactive or animated charts.
badges.story: Tell me about a famous visualisation you studied or recreated. What did it teach you about your own work?
badges.next: Build a small portfolio of two or three visualisations with a short note on each design choice.

badges.label: Analyst
badges.blurb: Read the patterns and test your explanations.
badges.cv: Identified patterns in data, framed testable hypotheses and made the assumptions behind my analysis explicit.
badges.story: Tell me about a finding from your project. How confident were you in it, and how did you explain its limits?
badges.next: Practise summarising a finding in one sentence for a non-specialist, then in one paragraph for an expert.

badges.label: Chart Repertoire
badges.blurb: More chart types, and when each one fits.
badges.cv: Chose from a wide range of chart types, including tree maps, radar, area and population pyramid charts, to suit the data and the question.
badges.story: Tell me about a time you chose a less familiar chart type. Why was it the right one?
badges.next: Keep a swipe file of chart types you see in the news, with a note on what each is good for.

trees.label: Critical Lens
trees.sub: On the age of data: one badge per lecture, up to your own essay

badges.label: The Age of Data
badges.blurb: Week 1: what the age of data is, and what it changes.
badges.cv: Placed my work in the wider context of the age of data and its consequences for society.
badges.story: Why does your project's topic matter now? What has changed because this data exists?
badges.reflect: Where in an ordinary day do you create data, and how much of it do you know about?

badges.label: The Data State
badges.blurb: Week 2: power, freedom and the birth of the data state.
badges.cv: Examined how states have used data to govern, and the trade-off between surveillance and freedom.
badges.story: Tell me about a time you weighed the benefits of collecting data against the risks to privacy.
badges.reflect: What do public bodies know about you, and how comfortable are you with that?

badges.label: Algorithms and Justice
badges.blurb: Week 3: oppressive algorithms, inequity and justice.
badges.cv: Evaluated how data and algorithms can encode bias and injustice, and who bears the harm.
badges.story: Give an example of data or an algorithm treating groups unfairly. How would you spot that in your own work?
badges.reflect: Has an automated decision ever affected you or someone you know? Would you know if it had?

badges.label: Seeing Data
badges.blurb: Week 4: the top 50 data visualisations of all time.
badges.cv: Decoded landmark visualisations to work out the data behind them, and how design can inform or mislead.
badges.story: Pick a famous chart. What data sits behind it, and what did its designer want you to see?
badges.reflect: Think of a chart that changed your mind about something. Should it have?

badges.label: Ideology and Metrics
badges.cv: Assessed what common metrics such as GDP capture and leave out, and the values built into them.
badges.story: Tell me about a measure you used in your project. What does it miss, and how did you deal with that?
badges.reflect: Which numbers do you use to judge your own life, such as grades, steps or followers? What do they leave out?

badges.label: Asking the People
badges.blurb: Week 7: social surveys, sex and what you ask.
badges.cv: Critically assessed social surveys: who is asked, how questions are worded and why the data was collected.
badges.story: Describe a survey you relied on. How confident were you in it, and why?
badges.reflect: When did you last answer a survey? Did the questions let you say what you meant?

badges.label: AI and the Data State
badges.blurb: Week 10: AI, capitalism and the future of the data state.
badges.cv: Considered how AI depends on data, and who gains and loses from data-driven technologies.
badges.story: How should someone in your future job think about using AI tools on data? What would you check?
badges.reflect: How do you use AI tools, and what do you check before trusting what they tell you?

badges.label: Sorting and Classifying
badges.blurb: Week 8: sorting and classifying, poverty and social class.
badges.cv: Questioned the categories data uses to sort people, including how poverty and social class are measured.
badges.story: Tell me about a category in your data that didn't fit reality neatly. What did you do?
badges.reflect: Which boxes have forms asked you to tick? Did any of them fit you badly?

badges.label: Polling and Democracy
badges.blurb: Week 9: politics, polling and who you ask.
badges.cv: Interpreted opinion polls critically, judging samples, margins of error and representativeness.
badges.story: A poll says 52% support a policy. What would you want to know before believing it?
badges.reflect: How do polls shape what you think other people believe?

badges.label: Data Humanist
badges.blurb: The peak: put your own project, and your essay, into the story of the age of data.
badges.cv: Situated my own data project within the history and politics of the age of data, and contributed to its study through an extended essay.
badges.story: How does your project, or your essay, add to our understanding of the age of data?
badges.reflect: What will you do differently with data now, as a citizen rather than a student?
badges.next: This is your distinctive edge as an arts, law or social sciences graduate: lead with it when applying for analytical roles.

badges.label: Excel User L1
badges.blurb: Spreadsheet basics: tidy, sort, filter, calculate.
badges.cv: Organised, cleaned and formatted data in Excel using tables, filters, sorting and formulae with relative and absolute references.
badges.story: Think of a time a spreadsheet you inherited or built was messy or unreliable. What did you do to make it usable, and how did you check it was right?
badges.next: Practise the keyboard shortcuts until they are automatic: speed and accuracy in Excel are noticed in almost any office role.

badges.label: Excel User L2
badges.cv: Used lookup, conditional and summary functions, pivot tables and Power Query to clean, combine and summarise datasets in Excel.
badges.story: When did you need an answer the raw data didn't give you directly? Which formulae or pivot tables did you use to get there?
badges.next: Learn XLOOKUP and INDEX/MATCH, which many workplaces now use in place of VLOOKUP.

badges.label: Excel User L3
badges.cv: Built interactive Excel outputs with pivot charts, calculated fields, slicers and conditional formatting.
badges.story: Describe something you built in Excel that other people could use without your help. How did you make it easy for them?
badges.next: Build a one-page interactive Excel dashboard from your project data and keep it as a portfolio piece.

badges.label: Tableau User L1
badges.cv: Imported data into Tableau and built charts using measures, dimensions and the Marks card.
badges.story: Why did you choose Tableau rather than Excel for a particular chart, and what difference did it make?
badges.next: Publish a chart to a free Tableau Public profile and link it from your CV or LinkedIn.

badges.label: Tableau User L2
badges.blurb: Dashboards, maps and stories in Tableau.
badges.cv: Created interactive Tableau dashboards, maps and stories, joining multiple datasets and exporting presentation-ready graphics.
badges.story: Walk me through a dashboard you built. Who was it for, and what did you want them to be able to find out for themselves?
badges.next: Tableau offers entry-level certifications if you want a formal credential to put on your CV.
